This is a '''list of cities in the United Kingdom''' that are officially designated as such {{as of|2022|8|29|lc=y}}.<ref name="govt_list">{{cite web |title=UK Cabinet Office List of Cities|url=https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20250509113712/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/list-of-cities/list-of-cities-html|access-date=10 June 2025|publication-date=29 August 2022|website=UK Government Web Archive}}</ref> It lists those places that have been granted [[City status in the United Kingdom|city status]] by [[letters patent]] or [[royal charter]].<ref name="govt_list" /><ref>{{cite news |last=McClatchey |first=Caroline |date=22 June 2011 |title=Why do towns want to become cities? |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-13841482 |access-date=5 August 2020}}</ref>

There are currently 76 such cities in the [[United Kingdom]]: 55 in England, [[List of towns and cities in Scotland by population|eight in Scotland]], [[list of cities in Wales|seven in Wales]], and six in [[Northern Ireland]].<ref name="govt_list" /> Of these, 24 in England, two in Wales, and two in Northern Ireland have [[Lord Mayor]]s; four in Scotland have [[Lord Provost]]s.{{efn|See [[List of lord mayoralties and lord provostships in the United Kingdom]].}} In some cases, the area holding city status does not coincide with the built up area or conurbation of which it forms part. In [[Greater London]], for example, the Cities of [[City of London|London]] and [[City of Westminster|Westminster]] hold city status separately, but no other local authority in the [[London Region]] has been granted city status, nor has the [[Greater London Authority]].

In other cases, such as the cities of [[City of Canterbury|Canterbury]] and [[City of Lancaster|Lancaster]], the status applies to a local government district which extends over a number of towns and rural areas outside the main settlement proper.{{sfnb|Beckett|2005}} In England, city status sometimes applies to [[civil parish]]es, such as with [[Ripon]]; though the status may not apply to the local government district which share their name. For example, the civil parishes of [[Lichfield]] and [[Chichester]] each hold city status, but [[Lichfield District]] and [[Chichester District]] in which they are situated do not.

As of 2022, there are currently five [[Ceremonial counties of England|ceremonial counties]] which contain three cities – [[Cambridgeshire]] (Ely, Cambridge and Peterborough{{Efn|Peterborough was in [[Northamptonshire]] from the Middle Ages until 1974.}}), [[Essex]], [[Hampshire]], [[West Midlands (county)|West Midlands]] and [[West Yorkshire]]. Outside the UK within [[British overseas cities]] of the [[British Overseas Territories]] and [[Crown Dependencies]], there are currently five. The number increased as part of the [[Platinum Jubilee of Elizabeth II|Platinum Jubilee]] celebrations by the addition of [[Stanley, Falkland Islands|Stanley]] in the [[Falkland Islands]] and [[Douglas, Isle of Man|Douglas]] in the [[Isle of Man]].

== History ==
{{hatnote|Main articles: [[City status in the United Kingdom]] and [[City status in Ireland|Ireland]], also [[Roman cities in Britain]].}}

The [[Roman Cities in Britain|earliest cities]] ({{langx|la|[[civitas]]}}) in [[Roman Britain|Britain]] were the fortified settlements organised by the [[Ancient Romans|Romans]] as capitals of the [[Celtic tribes of the British Isles|Celtic tribes]] under [[Britannia (Roman province)|Roman rule]]. The [[Britons (Celtic people)|British]] [[Celtic Christianity|clerics]] of the [[Sub-Roman Britain|early Middle Ages]] later preserved a traditional list of the "[[28 Cities of Britain|28 Cities]]" ({{langx|owl|[[caer|cair]]}}) which was mentioned in ''[[De Excidio Britanniae]]''{{efn|''[[s:la:De Excidio Britanniae|De Excidio Britanniae]]'', §3. {{in lang|la}} Cited in the "Civitas" entry of ''Celtic Culture''.<ref name=cc>{{cite encyclopedia |editor=John T Koch |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f899xH_quaMC&pg=PA451 |contribution=Civitas |title=Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia |volume=I |page=451 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |location=[[Santa Barbara, California]] |date=2006| isbn=978-1-85109-440-0 }}</ref>}} and ''[[Historia Brittonum]]''.<ref name=mommy>{{citation |editor-last=Mommsen |editor-first=Theodore |last=[[Nennius]] (Traditional attribution) |editor-link=Theodor Mommsen |chapter-url=https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/Historia_Brittonum#VI._CIVITATES_BRITANNIAE |chapter= VI. Civitates Britanniae |orig-date= Composed after AD&nbsp;830 |language=la |via=Latin Wikisource |title=Chronica Minora |series=Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Auctorum Antiquissimi xiii |location=Berlin |publisher=Weidmann |year=1898}}</ref>

The title of city was initially informal and, into the 20th century, royal charters were considered to ''recognise'' city status rather than grant it.{{efn|The [[1911 Encyclopædia Britannica|11th edition]] of the ''[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]'', for instance, listed [[St Asaph]] and [[Southwell, Nottinghamshire|Southwell]] as cities on the basis of their cathedrals despite their lack of charters or, in Southwell's case, local government.<ref>''Encyclopædia Britannica'', {{nowrap|11th ed.}} 1911.</ref>{{page needed|date= August 2024}}}} The usual criterion in [[early modern Britain]] was the presence of a [[cathedral]], particularly after [[Henry VIII of England|King Henry VIII]] granted [[letters patent]] establishing six new cities when he established a series of new [[list of Church of England dioceses|dioceses of the Church of England]] in the 1540s as part of the [[English Reformation]].{{sfnb|Beckett|2005|page=22}} No new cities were created between the 16th and 19th centuries, but following the [[Industrial Revolution in the United Kingdom|Industrial Revolution]] and the accompanying [[Population in Victorian England|population boom]] and growth in [[Urbanisation#History|urbanisation]], new [[episcopal see|sees]] were established at [[Ripon]] (1836) and [[Manchester]] (1847); their councils began to style them cities immediately. [[Inverness]] in Scotland was refused a charter at the time of the [[Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria]] honours of 1897, in part because it would have drawn more attention to the other traditional "cities" still not formally chartered as such.{{sfnb|Beckett|2005|p=61}}

Beginning in the mid-19th century, however, the process became more formal. After a visit by [[Queen Victoria]] in 1851, Manchester petitioned [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament]] for recognition of its status. Ripon followed in the 1860s, and a series of hitherto informal "cities" were formally recognised in the 1880s and 1890s. On the basis of its size, importance, and regular government, [[Belfast]] was elevated in spite of its lack of a cathedral in 1888; other large municipalities followed, while smaller applicants began to be rejected. King [[Edward VII]] and the [[Home Office]] established three criteria for future applicants in 1907: a minimum population of 300,000, a good record of local government, and a "local metropolitan character".{{sfnb|Beckett|2005|p=}} These criteria were not made public, however, and following [[Leicester]]'s successful elevation in 1919, a series of exceptions were made. The [[Local Government Act 1972]] effectively eliminated all authorities holding city status outside [[Greater London]] on 1 April 1974; most of their replacements were confirmed in their predecessor's status{{snd}} even in cases such as the [[Carlisle (district, 1974–2023)|1974&ndash;2023 Carlisle district]], where much of the local authority area was undeveloped countryside{{snd}} but the [[Borough of Medway]] was [[City status in the United Kingdom#Rochester|not permitted to continue Rochester's title]]. In recent times there have been [[City status in the United Kingdom#Current practice of granting city status|competitions]] for new grants of city status. Towns or councils that claim city status or add "city" to their name have been rebuked by the [[Advertising Standards Authority (United Kingdom)|Advertising Standards Authority]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.asa.org.uk/Rulings/Adjudications/2011/3/Medway-Council/TF_ADJ_49924.aspx |title=ASA Adjudication on Medway Council |publisher=Asa.org.uk |date=16 March 2011 |access-date=9 June 2016}}</ref>

The cities of the [[Kingdom of Scotland]] and [[Kingdom of Ireland]] were treated separately. Scottish towns irregularly applied the description to themselves, but were formally organised as [[royal burgh]]s; the special rights of these were preserved by Article XXI of the [[Treaty of Union]] which established the single state of the [[Kingdom of Great Britain]] in 1707.<ref>{{cite web|work=Kingdoms of England and Scotland |url=http://www.rahbarnes.demon.co.uk/Union/UnionWithEnglandAct.htm#XXI |title= "Act of Union", §XXI |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150226061820/http://www.rahbarnes.demon.co.uk/Union/UnionWithEnglandAct.htm#XXI |archive-date=26 February 2015 }}. 16 January 1707.</ref> [[Edinburgh]] and [[Glasgow]] were confirmed as cities "by ancient usage" in the 18th century,{{sfnb|Beckett|2005|p=}} as was [[Aberdeen]],{{sfnb|Beckett|2005|p=16}} and this was later reconfirmed in the Act enlarging the burgh in 1891. [[Dundee]] was granted [[letters patent]] in 1889 and [[Elgin, Moray|Elgin]] and [[Perth, Scotland|Perth]] were recognised as cities by the Home Office in 1972, before the privilege was removed by the [[Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973|Scottish Local Government Act]] of 1973.<ref name=privy>Clark, M. Lynda &&nbsp;al. [https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld199899/ldselect/ldprivi/108i/10811.htm "Committee on Privileges Second Report", Appendix 3, ss58]. Parliament of the United Kingdom (London), 1999.</ref> In Northern Ireland, only the seat of the [[Primate of All Ireland]] at [[Armagh]] was accorded city status by ancient usage, and this status was abolished by the [[Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act 1840]]. All other cities have been those explicitly recognised as such.

Thirty-two cities have a Lord Provost (in Scotland) or a Lord Mayor (in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland), see [[List of lord mayoralties and lord provostships in the United Kingdom]]. The six cities where the Lord Mayor or Lord Provost has the right to the style ''The Right Honourable'' are York, the City of London, Edinburgh, Glasgow (since 1912), Belfast (since 1923), and Cardiff (since 1956).

== Statistical role ==
{{Further|City status in the United Kingdom#Smallest and largest cities|City status in the United Kingdom#Populous towns}}
[[City status in the United Kingdom|City status]] has little statistical significance in the UK because it is not a measure of a city's size and only holds a ceremonial status. Historic cities, such as [[St Davids]] (a cathedral city in Wales) can be quite small, but newer cities, such as those [[City status in the United Kingdom|conferred in 2022]], can range in size from  50,000 to more than 200,000. Populous towns, such as [[Luton]], [[Northampton]] and [[Reading, Berkshire|Reading]], do not have city status.

=== Conurbations ===
The term "city" is sometimes loosely applied to [[conurbation]]s in the UK. The government tends to recognise these as [[primary urban area]]s for statistical and economic purposes, though [[List of urban areas in the United Kingdom|greater urban areas]] are what most people determine to be a city region.<ref>{{cite web |title=Does how we define cities change our understanding of them? | website=The Centre for Cities | url=https://www.centreforcities.org/blog/does-how-we-define-cities-change-our-understanding-of-them/ | date= 12 July 2021 |first=Paul |last=Swinney }}</ref> Large cities other than London, such as [[Manchester]] or [[Birmingham]], are often confused with these conurbations. Manchester has a significantly lower population than Birmingham, though the [[Greater Manchester Built-up Area]] is more populous than the [[West Midlands conurbation]].<ref name="E&Wdistricts2011">
{{cite web|title=2011 Census: KS101EW Usual resident population, local authorities in England and Wales|url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/rel/census/2011-census/key-statistics-for-local-authorities-in-england-and-wales/rft-table-ks101ew.xls|access-date=8 January 2013|publisher=[[Office for National Statistics]]}}
</ref> This question of definition has provoked a [[Second city of the United Kingdom|second city debate]] in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BBC Inside Out - |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/insideout/northwest/series11/week5_manchester_second_city.shtml |access-date=2025-03-24 |website=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref>

Conversely, many official cities in the UK contain a substantial rural area encompassing settlements which are physically separated from the core urban area. The [[City of Milton Keynes]] (a unitary authority) and [[City of Colchester]] (non-metropolitan district) received letters patent which covered an area substantially larger than that of their respective core urban areas; this meant that extra-urban settlements such as the towns of [[Olney, Buckinghamshire|Olney]]<ref>{{cite web| title= Milton Keynes celebrates City status |url= https://www.royal.uk/news-and-activity/2023-02-23/milton-keynes-celebrates-city-status| date= 23 February 2023| website=The Royal Family}}</ref> and [[West Mersea]] fall within ''de jure'' cities.<ref>{{cite web |title=Milton Keynes city status application |url=https://www.milton-keynes.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2022-06/Milton%20Keynes%20city%20status%20application.pdf | date= December 2021 |author=[[Milton Keynes City Council]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Colchester City Status|url=https://www.colchester.gov.uk/city-status/ | date= November 2022 |author=[[Colchester City Council]]}}</ref>

  "query":"SELECT DISTINCT\n  ?id\n  ?idLabel\n  ?countylabel\n  (0 AS ?fill_opacity)\n  (3 AS ?stroke_width)\n  (?countylabel AS ?title)\nWHERE {\n  ?id rdfs:label ?countylabel.\n  FILTER( LANG(?countylabel) IN (\"mul\", \"en\") )\n\n  FILTER(\n    ?id NOT IN (\n      wd:Q19186,\n      wd:Q929902,\n      wd:Q131467472\n    )\n  )\n\n  {\n    {\n      ?id p:P31 ?statement0.\n      ?statement0 (ps:P31/(wdt:P279*)) wd:Q180673.\n    }\n    UNION\n    {\n      ?id p:P31 ?statement1.\n      ?statement1 (ps:P31/(wdt:P279*)) wd:Q15060255.\n    }\n    UNION\n    {\n      ?id p:P31 ?statement2.\n      ?statement2 (ps:P31/(wdt:P279*)) wd:Q1317848.\n    }\n    UNION\n    {\n      ?id p:P31 ?statement5.\n      ?statement5 (ps:P31/(wdt:P279*)) wd:Q15979307.\n    }\n    UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P31) wd:Q141763519.          # city-status cities subclass\n  }\n    UNION\n    {\n      ?id p:P131 ?newport.\n      ?newport (ps:P131) wd:Q5283458.\n      ?id p:P31 ?newport2.\n      ?newport2 (ps:P31) wd:Q515.\n    }\n    UNION\n    {\n      ?id p:P131 ?scot.\n      ?scot (ps:P131) wd:Q22.\n      ?id p:P31 ?scot2.\n      ?scot2 (ps:P31) wd:Q515.\n    }\n    UNION\n    {\n      ?id p:P797 ?orkney.\n      ?orkney (ps:P797) wd:Q11994103.\n    }\n  }\n}\nLIMIT 200\n"
},
{
  "type": "ExternalData",
  "service": "geoshape",
  "query": "SELECT DISTINCT\n  ?id\n  ?idLabel\n  (\"#ff0000\" AS ?fill)\n  (0.3 AS ?fill_opacity)\n  (1 AS ?stroke_width)\n  (\"#ff0000\" AS ?stroke)\n  (0.7 AS ?stroke_opacity)\nWHERE {\n  { ?id rdfs:label ?idLabel. }\n  FILTER( LANG(?idLabel) IN (\"mul\", \"en\") )\n\n  FILTER(\n    ?id NOT IN (\n      wd:Q84, wd:Q1094110, wd:Q23154, wd:Q6226, wd:Q193452,\n      wd:Q22889, wd:Q269980, wd:Q1410, wd:Q211950,\n      wd:Q192896, wd:Q19840810\n    )\n  )\n\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statement0.\n    ?statement0 (ps:P31) wd:Q515.\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statement1.\n    ?statement1 (ps:P31) wd:Q27104997.\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statement2.\n    ?statement2 (ps:P31) wd:Q21503295.\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P279 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P279) wd:Q515.          # city-status cities subclass\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P131 ?newport.\n    ?newport (ps:P131) wd:Q11294004.\n    ?id p:P31 ?newport2.\n    ?newport2 (ps:P31) wd:Q515.\n  }\n\n  {\n    ?id p:P17 ?statement3.\n    ?statement3 (ps:P17) wd:Q145.\n  }\n}\nLIMIT 300\n"
},
{
  "type": "ExternalData",
  "service": "geopoint",
  "query": "SELECT DISTINCT  \n?id ?idLabel  \n?auth ?authLabel   \n?nogov ?nogovLabel   \n?geo ?link  \n(?img as ?img_)   \n(\"city\" AS ?marker_symbol)  \n(?category AS ?marker_color) \n(concat('[[w:', substr(str(?link),31,400),  '|', ?idLabel, ']]') as ?title)  \n(concat('', '[[File:', substr(str(?img_), 52, 400), '|200px]]') as ?description) \nWHERE {\n  SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language \"[AUTO_LANGUAGE],en, mul\". }\n\n  ### --- EXPANDED CITY SELECTOR ---\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statement0.\n    ?statement0 (ps:P31) wd:Q515.              # formal cities\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementS.\n    ?statementS (ps:P31) wd:Q110390579.        # list-based cities\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P31) wd:Q1867820.          # city-status cities\n  }\n    UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P279 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P279) wd:Q515.          # city-status cities subclass\n  }\n   UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P31) wd:Q141763519.          # city-status cities subclass\n  }\n  ### --------------------------------------------\n\n  ?id p:P17 ?statement1.\n  ?statement1 (ps:P17) wd:Q145.                # United Kingdom\n\n  ?id wdt:P625 ?geo.                           # coords\n\n  FILTER (?id NOT IN (\n    wd:Q84, wd:Q1410, wd:Q843868,\n    wd:Q24341876, wd:Q27573903, wd:Q19840810 # #remove non-formal cities and duplicates    \n  ))\n\n  OPTIONAL { ?id wdt:P18 ?img. } # image\n  OPTIONAL { ?link schema:about ?id; schema:isPartOf <https://en.wikipedia.org/>. }  #city wiki page  \n\n  OPTIONAL {\n    ?id wdt:P797 wd:Q3306606. #charter trustees      \n    BIND(?id AS ?auth)   #authority   \n  }\n\n  OPTIONAL {   ## pull in nogov cities   \n    {\n      SELECT DISTINCT ?id ?nogov\n      WHERE {\n        SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language \"[AUTO_LANGUAGE],mul,en\". }\n\n ### --- EXPANDED CITY SELECTOR ---\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statement2.\n    ?statement2 (ps:P31) wd:Q515.              # formal cities\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementU.\n    ?statementU (ps:P31) wd:Q110390579.        # list-based cities\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementV.\n    ?statementV (ps:P31) wd:Q1867820.          # city-status cities\n  }\n  UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P279 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P279) wd:Q515.          # city-status cities subclass\n  }\n   UNION\n  {\n    ?id p:P31 ?statementT.\n    ?statementT (ps:P31) wd:Q141763519.          # city-status cities subclass\n  }\n  ### --------------------------------------------\n\n        MINUS { ?id p:P31 ?statement3. ?statement3 (ps:P31) wd:Q17601336. }  #Not a district    \n\n        ?id p:P131 ?statement4.\n        ?statement4 (ps:P131/(wdt:P131)) ?region.\n        VALUES ?region { wd:Q22 wd:Q26 }   # In combined Scotland and Northern Ireland     \n\n        MINUS { ?id p:P31 ?statement5. ?statement5 (ps:P31) wd:Q1549591. } #Not a Big City #  \n\n        BIND(?id AS ?nogov)\n      }\n      LIMIT 20  #no gov less than at the moment     \n    }\n  }\n\n  BIND(\n    IF(\n      BOUND(?auth) && (?auth = ?id),\n      '#0057AF', #bound colour blue to charter trusts    \n      IF(\n        BOUND(?nogov) && (?id = ?nogov),\n        '#595959', #bound grey to no gov areas       \n        '#B60000' # bound red to everything else    \n      )\n    )\n    AS ?category\n  )\n}\nORDER BY ASC(?title) #arrange by title, bangor then gets correctly sorted by country   \nLIMIT 100 #total cities less than this\n"
},

    "title": "UKcities-nongov.map"
  }

== Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies ==
{{Main|British overseas cities}}
The [[British Overseas Territories]] and the [[Crown Dependencies]] do not form part of the [[United Kingdom]] but are part of its sovereign territory. Association of city status with cathedrals ended in 1865.{{sfnp|Beckett|2005|p=24}} There are presently five cities in the Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies.<ref name="O'Connor">{{cite news |date=20 May 2022 |title=Platinum Jubilee: Eight new cities created in Queen's honour |work=BBC News |last=O'Connor |first=Mary |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-61505857 |access-date=20 May 2022}}</ref>
